title: Jethro's advice (Exodus 18:13–27)
hook: his father-in-law says: you'll wear yourself out, share the load

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses on the hill with his arms getting heavy, and Aaron and Hur on either side. Your line was hold up their arms. Whose arms did you hold up? Day three hundred ninety-two, the end of week fifty-six.

A line has formed outside a tent in the desert. It started at sunrise. By noon it snakes past the cooking fires. A man wants to know whose goat it really was. Two cousins are fighting over a well. A widow has a complaint about her neighbor's fence, or the desert version of a fence. And at the front of the line, on a seat, sits one man hearing every single case himself: Moses. The people stand there, the text says, from the morning until the evening. Then an older man who has just arrived for a visit stands at the back and watches the whole day. He's Moses' father-in-law, Jethro, a priest from Midian. And when the long day is over, he says something nobody else has said.
screen: `A LINE OUTSIDE A TENT.` → `ONE MAN HEARS EVERY CASE.` → `AN OLD MAN WATCHES ALL DAY.`

segments.voice: Here is what Jethro says, in the King James Bible: "The thing that thou doest is not good." Blunt. Then the reason: "thou art not able to perform it thyself alone." He's not saying Moses is lazy or proud. He's saying this will wear him out, and wear the people out too, standing in that line all day. Then he offers a plan. Keep the hard cases, and the work of teaching the people the way. But find able people to judge the everyday ones, over groups of a thousand, a hundred, fifty and ten. And he says what kind of people: those who fear God, who tell the truth, who hate a bribe. Moses listens. He does exactly what his father-in-law says. Notice who gave the advice. Jethro isn't an Israelite. He's a priest of Midian, an outsider, and earlier in the chapter he hears the whole story of the rescue from Egypt and blesses God for it. The Bible lets a foreign father-in-law teach the great leader something about leadership, and it doesn't seem embarrassed at all. Jewish tradition honors him in a striking way: the weekly Torah reading that contains the Ten Commandments is named Yitro, after Jethro. Christians have read this chapter in many ways. Some churches point to it when they choose elders or deacons. Many people simply hear permission. Moses, who has talked with God at a burning bush, still can't carry a whole people alone. And that's been the shape of the whole week: a night of remembering, a hurried exit, a sea, a song, manna, tired arms held up, and now the load shared.
screen: `THIS IS NOT GOOD.` · `THOU ART NOT ABLE ALONE.` · `ABLE PEOPLE OVER TENS AND FIFTIES.` · `THE ADVICE CAME FROM AN OUTSIDER.` · then, large: `THOU ART NOT ABLE TO PERFORM IT THYSELF ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing to hand over. Settle, and breathe. Picture your own line outside the tent: everything that's waiting on you this week. Let it form, one thing at a time. Now look down the line for one item somebody else could do. Not badly. Just differently than you would. A task at work. A chore at home. A worry you've been carrying for a friend who could carry it themselves. Notice what makes it hard to let go. If you pray, you can ask for the Jethro in your life to speak up. The bell holds the time.
Jethro's advice. A father-in-law from Midian watches Moses judge alone from morning to evening and says: share the load, or it will wear you out.

Your line: you can't do it alone. Today, delegate one thing, out loud, to someone who can do it, and then leave it with them. And that's week fifty-six: Passover, haste, the sea, a tambourine, manna, tired arms, and Jethro. Day three hundred ninety-two.
screen: `WEEK FIFTY-SIX: PASSOVER · HASTE · THE SEA · A TAMBOURINE · MANNA · ARMS · JETHRO`

howItsDone: Many churches point to Exodus 18 when they appoint elders, deacons or lay leaders to share the work of a congregation, and pastors often cite Jethro's advice when talking about burnout and shared ministry.

fork.reveal: Moses listens and does everything Jethro said. the great leader takes advice from an outsider, and the text tells it without embarrassment.

original.note: Hebrew: Jethro's name. Jewish tradition names the Torah reading with the Ten Commandments after him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about delegating at work.
what it means: even Moses can't carry a whole people alone, and the wisdom to share the load comes from a priest of Midian.
what a scholar hears: Yitro, the name of the weekly Torah portion that runs from Jethro's visit through the giving of the Ten Commandments.

notes: Week fifty-six counted as days 386–392 (Passover night through Jethro). Confirm the week numbering and the look-back list.
Jethro's qualifications for judges (18:21: fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness) paraphrased as 'who hate a bribe'; confirm the paraphrase is fair.
Parashat Yitro covers Exodus 18:1–20:23 and includes the Ten Commandments; confirm.
Jethro is also called Reuel (Exodus 2:18) and Hobab is linked to him (Numbers 10:29; Judges 4:11); the script uses only 'Jethro'.
Claim that some churches cite Exodus 18 when choosing elders or deacons is general; confirm it is fair across traditions.

Hook details (the goat, the well, the widow's fence) are illustrative, not in the text. Jethro speaks after watching the day (18:13–14); 'that night' was changed to 'when the long day is over'. Confirm.
